docs.title: Pupil Labs Video
docs.text:
A high-level wrapper of PyAV providing an easy to use interface to video data.

The goal of this library is to provide a simple interface while maintaining good computational performance. At current, only MP4 and MJPEG videos are officially compatible.

Features include:

  • Performant reading of video files (optionally including audio) utilizing multi-threading.
  • Ability to arbitrarily index frames by their index or timestamp.
  • Ability to slice the video by frame index or time. Large slices will be loaded lazily to avoidexcessive RAM consumption.
  • A frame buffer is maintained to cache frames close to the current decoding position, which avoids repetitive seeking when going back and forth between frames in the same neighborhood or iterating backwards.
  • Avoids demuxing and seeking operations as much as possible.
  • Reading multi-part video files (e.g. how they are generated by Neon or Pupil Invisible).

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install pupil-labs-video

or

pip install -e git+https://github.com/pupil-labs/pl-video.git

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
You can open a video file and read frames like this:

import pupil_labs.video as plv

with plv.Reader(video_path) as video:
    # Iterate through video frames
    for frame in video:
        # Convert video frame to BGR array
        img = frame.bgr

    # Index individual frames or slices
    first_frame = video[0]
    last_frame = video[-1]
    frames = video[10:20]

    # Index frames by time
    ts = video[10].time
    frame = video.by_container_timestamps[ts]
    frames = video.by_container_timestamps[ts : ts + 10]

You can write video files like this:

import pupil_labs.video as plv

with (plv.Writer(out_path) as writer):
    for img in images:
        writer.write_image(img)

docs.title: The new reader
docs.text:
pupil_labs.video_reader is a reader for MP4 files that seeks from the frame table the file already holds, so any frame of a long video is a fraction of a second away. It is indexed like a numpy array, as docs/adr/0001-the-reader-is-indexed-like-a-numpy-array.md records:

import numpy as np
from pupil_labs.video_reader import Reader

with Reader(video_path) as video:
    frame = video[-1]  # one frame: index, time, pts, bgr, rgb, gray
    every_tenth = video[::10]  # a Selection: nothing decoded yet
    picked = video[[5, 3, 5]]  # any order, repeats allowed
    later = video[video.timestamps > 10.0]  # a Boolean mask
    for frame in every_tenth:  # several keyframe groups decode at once
        img = frame.bgr
    at_12_5_s = video[np.searchsorted(video.timestamps, 12.5)]  # a frame by time

It needs Python 3.13. Two commands hold it to pl-video's Reader on the videos under /mnt/data/recordings and tests/data (git lfs pull first):

  • make compare compares index, time, pts, .bgr, .rgb and .gray of every frame and lists each mismatch.
  • make benchmark times both readers per scenario and video, five fresh processes each, and checks the new one is no slower and uses no more memory.

def __init__(
    self,
    source: Path | str,
    stream: Literal["audio", "video"]
    | tuple[Literal["audio", "video"], int] = "video",
    container_timestamps: ContainerTimestamps | list[float] | None | None = None,
    logger: Logger | None = None,
):
    """Create a reader for a video file.

    Args:
        source: Path to a video file. Can be a local path or an http-address.
        stream: The stream to read from, either "audio", "video". If the video file
            contains multiple streams of the deisred kind, a tuple can be provided
            to specify which stream to use, e.g. `("audio", 2)` to use the audio
            stream at index `2`.
        container_timestamps: Array containing the timestamps of the video frames in
            container time (equal to PTS * time_base). If not provided, timestamps
            will be inferred from the container. Providing pre-loaded values can
            speed up initialization for long videos by avoiding demuxing of the
            entire video to obtain PTS.
        logger: Python logger to use. Decreases performance.

    """
    self._container_timestamps: ContainerTimestamps | None = None
    if container_timestamps is not None:
        if isinstance(container_timestamps, list):
            container_timestamps = np.array(container_timestamps)
        self.container_timestamps = container_timestamps

    self.lazy_frame_slice_limit = LAZY_FRAME_SLICE_LIMIT
    self._times_were_provided = container_timestamps is not None
    self._source = source
    self._logger = logger or DEFAULT_LOGGER
    self.stats = Stats()

    if not isinstance(stream, tuple):
        stream = (stream, 0)
    self._stream_kind, self._stream_index = stream

    self._log = bool(logger)
    self._is_at_start = True
    self._last_processed_dts = -maxsize
    self._partial_pts = list[int]()
    self._partial_dts = list[int]()
    self._partial_dts_to_index = dict[int, int]()
    self._partial_pts_to_index = dict[int, int]()
    self._all_pts_are_loaded = False
    self._decoder_frame_buffer = list[SortableFrame]()
    self._current_decoder_index: int | None = -1
    self._indexed_frames_buffer: deque[ReaderFrameType] = deque(maxlen=1000)
    self._reorder_buffer_size = 10

    # this forces loading the gopsize on initialization to set the buffer length
    assert self.gop_size

    # TODO: this can be set to gop size but tests need adapting
    self._reorder_buffer_size = 35

docs.title: by_container_timestamps cached property
docs.text:
by_container_timestamps: Indexer[ReaderFrameType]

Time-based access to video frames using container timestamps.

Container time is measured in seconds relative to begining of the video. Accordingly, the first frame typically has timestamp 0.0.

When accessing a specific key, e.g. reader[t], a frame with this exact timestamp needs to exist, otherwise an IndexError is raised. When acessing a slice, e.g. reader[a:b] an ArrayLike is returned such that a <= frame.time < b for every frame.

Large slices are returned as a lazy view, which avoids immediately loading all frames into RAM.

Note that numerical imprecisions of float numbers can lead to issues when accessing individual frames by their container timestamp. It is recommended to prefer indexing frames via slices.

def __init__(
    self,
    path: str | Path,
    lossless: bool = False,
    fps: int | None = None,
    bit_rate: int = 2_000_000,
    logger: Logger | None = None,
) -> None:
    """Video writer for creating videos from image arrays.

    Args:
        path: The path to write the video to.
        lossless: If True, the video will be encoded in lossless H264.
        fps: The desired framerate of the video.
        bit_rate: The desired bit rate of the video.
        logger: Python logger to use. Decreases performance.

    """
    self.path = path
    self.lossless = lossless
    self.fps = fps
    self.bit_rate = bit_rate
    self.logger = logger or DEFAULT_LOGGER
    self.container = av.open(self.path, "w")

def write_image(
    self,
    image: npt.NDArray[np.uint8],
    time: float | None = None,
    pix_fmt: PixelFormat | None = None,
) -> None:
    """Write an image to the video.

    Args:
        image: The image to write. Can have 1 or 3 channels.
        time: The time of the frame in seconds.
        pix_fmt: The pixel format of the image. If None, the pixel format will be
            `gray` for 1-channel images and `bgr24` for 3-channel images.

    """
    if pix_fmt is None:
        pix_fmt = "bgr24"
        if image.ndim == 2:
            pix_fmt = "gray"

    frame = av.VideoFrame.from_ndarray(image, str(pix_fmt))
    self.write_frame(frame, time=time)

docs.title: The reader is indexed like a numpy array
docs.text:
pupil_labs.video_reader.Reader takes the one-dimensional keys numpy takes, with numpy's meaning: reader[i] is one frame for a Python or numpy integer, negative ones counting from the end. A slice with any step, a Boolean mask as long as the reader, or a list or array of indices returns a Selection, which behaves like [reader[i], reader[k]] but decodes nothing until a frame is asked for. A selection takes the same keys, so reader[10:100][::2][3] is reader[16], and its indices are copied and checked when it is made. A frame's index is its position in the video, whatever selection it came from. Every key's result and error match what the key selects from np.arange(len(reader)); a lone Boolean and a zero-dimensional array raise, because numpy gives them meanings a sequence of frames cannot have.

pl-video's Reader took an integer or a slice, ignored a slice's step, returned a list for slices under 30 frames, and offered access by timestamp through by_container_timestamps.

docs.title: Considered Options
docs.text:
• A named method for index arrays and masks, or integer access only. Proposed in review to keep __getitem__'s typing simple. Rejected: a selection that knows all its targets lets the reader plan the decode, several keyframe groups at once, and the typing has a fix: the frame overload takes int | np.integer, not anything usable as an index, so reader[np.int64(3)] types as a frame and reader[np.arange(3)] as a selection.
  • A list for short slices, as pl-video did. Rejected: one return type is simpler to type and to use.
  • Access by timestamp. Dropped. Nothing in Neon X or pl-neon-recording called it, a single timestamp had to match a float exactly, and a slice ignored its step. Callers find the index with np.searchsorted(reader.timestamps, t) and use reader[i].
  • Indexing into a frame's pixels through the reader (reader[i, :, :10]). Left out: keys are one-dimensional.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• How a reader of several files relabels a frame's index and time is decided when one is built; adding a way to copy a frame then breaks nothing.
  • reader[True] is a TypeError, although bool is an int to the type checker.
